\begin{theorem}[Divisibility law]\label{thm:dvdlaw}
For $m \ge 1$ and all $n \ge 0$, $\ m \mid P_n \iff \rank(m) \mid n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
($\Leftarrow$) If $\rank(m)\mid n$ then $P_{\rank(m)} \mid P_n$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:dvdiff}, and $m \mid P_{\rank(m)}$ by definition.

($\Rightarrow$) Assume $m \mid P_n$ with $n>0$ (the case $n=0$ being trivial), and put $r = \rank(m)$. Then $m$ divides $\gcd(P_r,P_n) = P_{\gcd(r,n)}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:sd}. As $\gcd(r,n)>0$, minimality of $r$ gives $r \le \gcd(r,n)$; and $\gcd(r,n)\le r$ trivially. Hence $\gcd(r,n)=r$, i.e.\ $r \mid n$.
\end{proof}

This is where the two halves of the theory meet: pigeonhole supplies existence, strong divisibility supplies rigidity, and minimality clicks them together.

\begin{theorem}[Multiplicativity]\label{thm:mult}
If $a,b\ge1$ are coprime then $\rank(ab) = \lcmop(\rank(a),\rank(b))$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
For any $n$: $\rank(ab)\mid n \iff ab \mid P_n \iff (a \mid P_n$ and $b \mid P_n) \iff (\rank(a)\mid n$ and $\rank(b)\mid n) \iff \lcmop(\rank a,\rank b)\mid n$, using coprimality and Theorem~\ref{thm:dvdlaw}. Two positive integers with the same set of multiples are equal.
\end{proof}

Hence $\rank$ is determined by its values on prime powers.

\begin{refutation}[Conjecture E]
\emph{For every odd prime $p$, $\rank(p) \mid p-1$ (equivalently $p \mid P_{p-1}$).} \textbf{False}: $p=3$ has $\rank(3)=4$ and $4 \nmid 2$; equivalently $3 \nmid P_2 = 2$. Note $4 \mid p+1$: the conjecture chose the wrong side, and \S\ref{sec:fermat} proves the correct dichotomy.
\end{refutation}

\begin{refutation}[Conjecture G]
\emph{For every prime $p$, $\rank(p^2) = p\,\rank(p)$.} \textbf{False}: since $P_7 = 169 = 13^2$ we have $\rank(169) = \rank(13) = 7 \neq 91$.
\end{refutation}

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:31}
$31^2 \mid P_{30} = 107\,578\,520\,350$ and $\rank(31) = \rank(961) = 30$. Hence at least two primes satisfy $\rank(p^2) = \rank(p)$, namely $13$ and $31$.
\end{proposition}

\section{A Fermat law via Frobenius in $\Z[\sqrt2]$}\label{sec:fermat}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:zsqrt2}
In $\Z[\sqrt2]$ one has $(1+\sqrt2)^n = Q_n + P_n\sqrt2$, and $(\sqrt2)^{2m+1} = 2^m\sqrt2$ for $m \ge 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{theorem}[Euler's criterion on the spine]\label{thm:euler}
Let $p = 2m+1$ be an odd prime. Then
\[
P_p \equiv 2^m = 2^{(p-1)/2} \pmod p, \qquad Q_p \equiv 1 \pmod p .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
In any commutative ring and for any prime $p$ there is an element $r$ with $(x+y)^p = x^p+y^p+p\,xy\,r$, because $p \mid \binom{p}{k}$ for $0<k<p$. Apply this in $\Z[\sqrt2]$ with $x=1$, $y = \sqrt2$:
\[
(1+\sqrt2)^p = 1 + (\sqrt2)^p + p\sqrt2\,r = 1 + 2^m\sqrt2 + p\sqrt2\,r .
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:zsqrt2} the left side is $Q_p + P_p\sqrt2$. Since $\{1,\sqrt2\}$ is a $\Z$-basis, comparing coordinates gives $Q_p = 1 + pr_0$ and $P_p = 2^m + pr_1$ for integers $r_0,r_1$.
\end{proof}

By Euler's criterion, $2^{(p-1)/2}\equiv \legendre{2}{p} \pmod p$, which is $+1$ exactly when $p \equiv \pm1 \pmod 8$. So the congruence already carries the quadratic-residue information that Conjecture E ignored.

\begin{theorem}[Fermat law for the Pell spine]\label{thm:fermat}
For every odd prime $p$, $\ p \mid P_{p-1}P_{p+1}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
By Theorem~\ref{thm:euler} and Fermat's little theorem, $P_p^2 \equiv 2^{p-1}\equiv 1 \pmod p$. Theorem~\ref{thm:cassini} with $n = p-1$ gives $P_{p+1}P_{p-1} - P_p^2 = (-1)^{p}= -1$ for odd $p$, i.e.\ $P_{p-1}P_{p+1} = P_p^2-1$. Hence $p \mid P_{p-1}P_{p+1}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}\label{cor:fermatside}
For every odd prime $p$: $p \mid P_{p-1}$ or $p \mid P_{p+1}$; equivalently $\rank(p)\mid p-1$ or $\rank(p)\mid p+1$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
$p$ is prime, so it divides one of the two factors of Theorem~\ref{thm:fermat}; apply Theorem~\ref{thm:dvdlaw}.
\end{proof}

Corollary~\ref{cor:fermatside} is the repaired form of Conjecture E; the uniform statement is $\rank(p)\mid p - \legendre{2}{p}$, and $p=3$ is simply the case $\legendre{2}{3} = -1$, where indeed $\rank(3)=4 \mid 4 = p+1$.

\section{The companion strand: a parity-graded law}\label{sec:companion}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:units}
(i) $Q_n$ is odd for all $n$. (ii) $\gcd(Q_m, 2P_m^2) = 1$. (iii) $Q_m \mid P_{2m}$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
(i) Induction using $Q_{n+1}=Q_n+2P_n$. (ii) $Q_m$ is odd by (i) and coprime to $P_m$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:coprime}. (iii) $P_{2m}=2P_mQ_m$ by Corollary~\ref{cor:double}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Companion divisibility law]\label{thm:qdvd}
For $m \ge 2$ and any $n$,
\[
Q_m \mid Q_n \iff n = mk \ \text{ for some odd } k .
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The proof splits into two independent halves.

\emph{Index step.} From $Q_m \mid Q_n$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:units}(iii) at $m$ and $n$ one deduces $Q_m \mid \gcd(P_{2m},P_{2n}) = P_{2\gcd(m,n)}$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:sd}. If $g = \gcd(m,n) < m$ then $g \mid m$ forces $2g \le m$, so $0 < P_{2g} \le P_m < Q_m$ (using $Q_m = P_m+P_{m-1}>P_m$ for $m \ge 2$), contradicting $Q_m \mid P_{2g}$. Hence $m \mid n$.

\emph{Parity step.} Modulo $Q_m$, the addition law \eqref{eq:add} gives $Q_{a+2m} = Q_aQ_{2m}+2P_aP_{2m} \equiv 2P_m^2\,Q_a$, using $Q_{2m} = Q_m^2+2P_m^2$ and $Q_m \mid P_{2m}$. Iterating from $a=0$ yields $Q_{2jm}\equiv (2P_m^2)^j \pmod{Q_m}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:units}(ii) the base is a unit modulo $Q_m$, so the right side is never $0$; hence $Q_m \nmid Q_{2jm}$. Combined with Proposition~\ref{prop:oddmult} and the index step, the equivalence follows.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Companion gcd law]\label{thm:qgcd}
For all $m,n$, writing $g = \gcd(m,n)$,
\[
\gcd(Q_m,Q_n) = \begin{cases} Q_g, & \text{if } m/g \text{ and } n/g \text{ are both odd},\\ 1, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
If both quotients are odd, Proposition~\ref{prop:oddmult} gives $Q_g \mid Q_m$ and $Q_g \mid Q_n$, hence $Q_g \mid \gcd(Q_m,Q_n)$; the reverse divisibility follows from the index step of Theorem~\ref{thm:qdvd} together with minimality of $g$.

Suppose instead $m/g$ is even. Let $p$ be a prime dividing $\gcd(Q_m,Q_n)$ and put $r = \rank(p)$. From $p \mid Q_m \mid P_{2m}$ we get $r \mid 2m$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:dvdlaw}, likewise $r \mid 2n$, so $r \mid 2g$. But $p \nmid P_m$ since $\gcd(P_m,Q_m)=1$, so $r \nmid m$, in particular $r \nmid g$. From $r \mid 2g$ and $r \nmid g$ we get $v_2(r) = v_2(g)+1$ and that the odd part of $r$ divides $g$. Since $m/g$ is even, $v_2(m)\ge v_2(g)+1 = v_2(r)$, and the odd part of $r$ divides $g \mid m$; hence $r \mid m$, a contradiction. So $\gcd(Q_m,Q_n)$ has no prime divisor.
\end{proof}

Theorem~\ref{thm:qgcd} has \emph{no} side conditions: it is a complete replacement for the false Conjecture D. The structure is not a failure of strong divisibility but a grading of it by the parity of index quotients, traceable to the sign $(-1)^n$ in \eqref{eq:norm}.

\begin{refutation}[Conjectures D$'$, D$''$]
\emph{$Q_n \mid Q_{kn}$ for all $k$}, and \emph{$m \mid n \Rightarrow Q_m \mid Q_n$}. Both \textbf{false}: $Q_2 = 3 \nmid 17 = Q_4$.
\end{refutation}

\begin{proposition}[Summation identities]\label{prop:sums}
For all $n$,
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n}Q_i = P_{n+1}, \qquad 2\sum_{i=0}^{n}P_i + 1 = P_{n+1}+P_n, \qquad 2\sum_{i=0}^{n}P_i^2 = P_nP_{n+1}.
\]
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Each is a one-line induction using Lemma~\ref{lem:onestep}; the first telescopes because $P_{n+2}-P_{n+1}=Q_{n+1}$.
\end{proof}

\section{Diophantine classification}\label{sec:dioph}

\begin{lemma}[Descent]\label{lem:descent}
If $x,y \ge 0$ are integers with $x^2-2y^2 = \pm1$ and $y \ge 2$, then $(x',y') = (3x-4y,\,3y-2x)$ consists of non-negative integers with $x'^2-2y'^2 = x^2-2y^2$ and $y' < y$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The map is multiplication by $3-2\sqrt2 = (1+\sqrt2)^{-2}$, which preserves the norm. Non-negativity and the strict decrease $3y-2x<y$ follow from $x^2 = 2y^2\pm1$ with $2y^2 \ge 8$, which pins $x/y$ close enough to $\sqrt2$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Classification of units]\label{thm:units}
For non-negative integers $x,y$,
\[
\bigl(x^2 = 2y^2+1 \ \text{ or }\ x^2+1 = 2y^2\bigr) \iff \exists n:\ (x,y) = (Q_n,P_n).
\]
Moreover $x^2 = 2y^2+1$ corresponds exactly to even $n$ and $x^2+1 = 2y^2$ exactly to odd $n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
($\Leftarrow$) is Theorem~\ref{thm:norm}. ($\Rightarrow$): strong induction on $y$ via Lemma~\ref{lem:descent}, with base cases $y \in \{0,1\}$ giving $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$; climbing back by multiplication by $(1+\sqrt2)^2 = 3+2\sqrt2$ recovers the index, shifted by two, so parity is preserved and matches the sign of the norm.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[A local obstruction]\label{prop:mod8}
There are no integers with $x^2 = 2y^2+3$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
Modulo $8$, squares lie in $\{0,1,4\}$, while $2y^2+3 \in \{3,5\}$.
\end{proof}

\begin{refutation}[Conjecture H]
\emph{The form $x^2-2y^2$ represents no value other than $\pm1$ over the non-negative integers.} \textbf{False}: $3^2-2\cdot1^2 = 7$. Together with Proposition~\ref{prop:mod8} this shows the represented values are cut out by congruence conditions modulo $8$, not by size: $7$ is represented, $3$ is not.
\end{refutation}

\begin{theorem}[Near-isosceles triples]\label{thm:nearisos}
For non-negative integers $a,c$,
\[
a^2 + (a+1)^2 = c^2 \iff \exists k:\ 2a+1 = Q_{2k+1} \ \text{and}\ c = P_{2k+1}.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Completing the square, $a^2+(a+1)^2 = c^2$ is equivalent to $(2a+1)^2+1 = 2c^2$. With $x = 2a+1$, $y = c$ this is the negative Pell equation, whose solutions are the odd-index spine points by Theorem~\ref{thm:units}. Conversely $Q_{2k+1}$ is odd, so $a = (Q_{2k+1}-1)/2$ is an integer.
\end{proof}

The list begins $(0,1,1),(3,4,5),(20,21,29),(119,120,169),(696,697,985),(4059,4060,5741),\dots$

\begin{proposition}\label{prop:mod4}
Every near-isosceles hypotenuse satisfies $P_{2k+1}\equiv 1 \pmod 4$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction using $P_{n+4} = 6P_{n+2}-P_n$, which modulo $4$ reads $P_{n+4}\equiv 2P_{n+2}-P_n$; with $P_1 = 1$ and $P_3 = 5 \equiv 1$ the odd-index residues remain $1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{refutation}[Conjecture F]
\emph{The hypotenuse of a near-isosceles Pythagorean triple is prime.} \textbf{False}: $119^2+120^2 = 169^2$ and $169 = 13^2$. A geometric statement destroyed by the same arithmetic accident $P_7 = 169$ that killed Conjectures A, B and C.
\end{refutation}

\section{Diophantine approximation}\label{sec:approx}

\begin{lemma}\label{lem:conj}
$(1-\sqrt2)^n = Q_n - P_n\sqrt2$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Apply the ring automorphism $\sqrt2 \mapsto -\sqrt2$ of $\Z[\sqrt2]$ to \eqref{eq:spine}.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Exact error]\label{thm:error}
For all $n$, $\ \bigl|Q_n - P_n\sqrt2\bigr| = (\sqrt2-1)^n$, and $Q_n - P_n\sqrt2$ has sign $(-1)^n$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Take absolute values in Lemma~\ref{lem:conj}; $|1-\sqrt2| = \sqrt2-1 \in (0,1)$, and $(1-\sqrt2)^n$ has sign $(-1)^n$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Dirichlet quality]\label{thm:dirichlet}
For $n \ge 1$, $\ \left|\sqrt2 - \dfrac{Q_n}{P_n}\right| < \dfrac{1}{P_n^2}$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Dividing Theorem~\ref{thm:error} by $P_n$, it suffices that $P_n(\sqrt2-1)^n<1$. From the Binet formula $P_n = \bigl((1+\sqrt2)^n-(1-\sqrt2)^n\bigr)/(2\sqrt2)$ and $(1+\sqrt2)(\sqrt2-1)=1$ one gets $P_n(\sqrt2-1)^n = \bigl(1-(1-\sqrt2)^{2n}\bigr)/(2\sqrt2) < 1/\sqrt2 < 1$.
\end{proof}

\begin{refutation}[Conjectures I, J]
\emph{$|\sqrt2-Q_n/P_n| < 1/(3P_n^2)$ for all $n\ge1$}: \textbf{false} at $n=1$, where the error is $|\sqrt2-1| = 0.41421\dots > 1/3$. \emph{The convergents approach $\sqrt2$ from one side}: \textbf{false}, since $Q_1/P_1 = 1 < \sqrt2 < 3/2 = Q_2/P_2$.
\end{refutation}

Numerically $P_n^2|\sqrt2 - Q_n/P_n| \to 1/(2\sqrt2) = 0.353553\dots$, from above along even $n$ and from below along odd $n$: the constant $1$ is not asymptotically optimal, but it \emph{is} optimal as a statement valid for every $n \ge 1$, because of the exceptional first term. Parity again decides the side.

\section{The Wall--Sun--Sun phenomenon on the Pell spine}\label{sec:wss}

\subsection{Background}

For the Fibonacci sequence, define the rank of apparition $\rank_F(m)$ analogously. Classically $\rank_F(p^2)\in\{\rank_F(p),\,p\,\rank_F(p)\}$, with the second alternative generic. A prime realising the first --- equivalently $p^2 \mid F_{\rank_F(p)}$ --- is a \textbf{Wall--Sun--Sun prime}. Such primes are relevant to the first case of Fermat's Last Theorem, and extensive computation has found none below $10^{17}$. The same dichotomy holds on the Pell spine: $\rank(p^2)$ is either $\rank(p)$ or $p\,\rank(p)$, since $\rank(p)\mid \rank(p^2)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:dvdlaw} while $p^2 \mid P_{p\rank(p)}$ always.

\subsection{Two Pell--Wall--Sun--Sun primes}

\begin{theorem}\label{thm:wss}
$\rank(13) = \rank(169) = 7$ and $\rank(31) = \rank(961) = 30$. Hence Conjecture G is false, and $13$, $31$ are Pell--Wall--Sun--Sun primes.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
$P_7 = 169 = 13^2$, so $\rank(169)\le 7$; as $\rank(169)$ is a multiple of $\rank(13) = 7$ (checking $P_1,\dots,P_6$), we get $\rank(169)=7$. Similarly $P_{30} = 107\,578\,520\,350 = 2\cdot5^2\cdot7\cdot29\cdot31^2\cdot41\cdot269$, so $31^2 \mid P_{30}$; checking $P_1,\dots,P_{29}$ modulo $31$ gives $\rank(31)=30$, whence $\rank(961)=30$.
\end{proof}

\subsection{Density heuristic}

The standard heuristic models $P_{\rank(p)}/p \bmod p$ as uniform in $\Z/p$, predicting that $p$ is a Wall--Sun--Sun prime with probability $1/p$ and hence a counting function of order $\log\log x$. The Pell spine has an extra structural feature: the discriminant of $\Z[\sqrt2]$ is $8$, so the prime $2$ is \emph{ramified}, which is absent in the Fibonacci case (discriminant $5$) and heuristically doubles the density constant. Two hits below $10^2$ remains a small-numbers phenomenon, but it is consistent with a doubled constant and makes the Pell setting a far more tractable laboratory.

\begin{conjecture}[Open]\label{conj:density}
The set of Pell--Wall--Sun--Sun primes is infinite, with counting function asymptotic to $c\log\log x$; its first two elements are $13$ and $31$.
\end{conjecture}

\subsection{The $P_7 = 169$ singularity}

Five conjectures --- drawn from elementary primality, factorisation theory, plane geometry and the arithmetic of ranks --- are destroyed by the same integer. Arithmetic accidents in a linear recurrence are visible from many directions at once, because the conjectures are all pulled back from the same underlying factorisation event. Methodologically, one should locate a sequence's accidents first and then test all conjectures against them.

\section{Algorithms}

All algorithms below work modulo $m$ and never form the exponentially large Pell numbers.

\begin{algorithm}[Pell modulo $m$]
Iterate $(a,b)\leftarrow (b,\,2b+a) \bmod m$ from $(0,1)$: cost $O(n)$ modular operations and $O(\log m)$ space. A fast variant uses $P_{2n}=2P_nQ_n$, $Q_{2n}=Q_n^2+2P_n^2$, $P_{2n+1}=P_{2n}+Q_{2n}$, $Q_{2n+1}=Q_{2n}+2P_{2n}$, giving $O(\log n)$ multiplications.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Rank of apparition]
Iterate the previous algorithm and return the first $n>0$ with $P_n\equiv0$; termination is guaranteed by Theorem~\ref{thm:app} with the a priori bound $n \le m^2$. In practice, Theorem~\ref{thm:mult} reduces to prime powers, and for a prime $p$ Corollary~\ref{cor:fermatside} restricts $\rank(p)$ to divisors of $p \mp 1$, so only $O(d(p\mp1))$ modular exponentiations are needed.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Pell--Wall--Sun--Sun search]
For each prime $p \le X$: compute $\rank(p)$, then $P_{\rank(p)} \bmod p^2$, and report $p$ when the result is $0$. With the divisor-restricted rank computation the total cost is $\tilde O(X)$.
\end{algorithm}

\begin{algorithm}[Near-isosceles triple generator]
Iterate $(x,y)\leftarrow(3x+4y,\,2x+3y)$ from $(1,1)$; each state yields the triple $\bigl(\frac{x-1}{2},\frac{x+1}{2},y\bigr)$. This is multiplication by $\delta^2 = 3+2\sqrt2$ and produces all such triples exactly once, by Theorem~\ref{thm:nearisos}.
\end{algorithm}

\section{Applications}

\textbf{Continued fractions.} Theorem~\ref{thm:error} gives the exact error of the convergents of $\sqrt2 = [1;2,2,2,\dots]$, with geometric rate $(\sqrt2-1)^n$ and alternating sign --- no asymptotic notation required.

\textbf{Primality testing.} Corollary~\ref{cor:fermatside} supplies a Lucas-style compositeness test: for odd primes, $P_{p-\legendre{2}{p}} \equiv 0 \pmod p$. Composites passing it are Pell pseudoprimes; combined Fermat-plus-Lucas tests of this shape underpin widely used probable-prime routines.

\textbf{Rational triangle geometry.} Theorem~\ref{thm:nearisos} generates the right triangles closest to isosceles, with growth ratio $\delta^2 \approx 5.83$ between consecutive triples, and Proposition~\ref{prop:mod4} places all their hypotenuses in the class $1 \bmod 4$.

\textbf{Unit groups.} Theorem~\ref{thm:units} is the coordinate-level form of Dirichlet's unit theorem for $\Z[\sqrt2]$: the totally positive solutions of $|x^2-2y^2|=1$ form a cyclic monoid generated by $(1,1)$.

\section{Discussion}

\textbf{Norm versus trace.} Strong divisibility is a property of the norm-form sequence $P$ --- the $y$-solutions of $x^2-2y^2=\pm1$ --- and not of the trace sequence $Q$. On $Q$ it degrades to the parity-graded laws of Theorems~\ref{thm:qdvd} and \ref{thm:qgcd}. For companion pairs of Lucas sequences one should expect the two strands to obey different divisibility theories related by a grading rather than an identity.

\textbf{Parity as hidden variable.} The sign $(-1)^n$ in \eqref{eq:norm} simultaneously controls which Pell equation the spine point solves, which side of $\sqrt2$ the convergent lies on, whether the index yields a near-isosceles triple, and whether $Q_m \mid Q_n$ can hold.

\textbf{Accidents cluster.} One term, $P_7 = 169$, falsifies five conjectures across four subject areas; computer-assisted conjecture testing should therefore search for arithmetic accidents first.

\textbf{On the methodology.} Each refuted conjecture produced a sharper theorem: Conjecture E produced Corollary~\ref{cor:fermatside} and the Legendre symbol; Conjecture D produced Theorem~\ref{thm:qgcd}, which is stronger than what it replaced in having no side conditions; Conjecture G produced Theorem~\ref{thm:wss} and a concrete instance of a phenomenon undetected in the Fibonacci setting. A conjecture stated so that one number can kill it is a conjecture whose death is informative.

\section{Future directions}

\textbf{Silver-ratio Wall--Sun--Sun density.} Conjecture~\ref{conj:density}. The ramification of $2$ in $\Z[\sqrt2]$, absent in the Fibonacci setting, plausibly doubles the density constant, explaining why two examples appear below $50$ here and none below $10^{17}$ there. With Theorems~\ref{thm:dvdlaw} and \ref{thm:mult} in place a search can be organised prime by prime with certified intermediate steps.

\textbf{Parity-graded divisibility for general companion spines.} The Pell case is settled. Let $V$ be the companion sequence of the Lucas pair $(a,-1)$: $V_0=2$, $V_1=a$, $V_{n+2}=aV_{n+1}+V_n$. Conjecturally, for $g = \gcd(m,n)$, $\gcd(V_m,V_n) = V_g$ when $m/g$ and $n/g$ are both odd, and is bounded by a small explicit constant otherwise.

\textbf{Prime-power ranks.} By Theorem~\ref{thm:mult} the rank function is determined on prime powers. Establishing the dichotomy $\rank(p^{k+1})\in\{\rank(p^k),\,p\,\rank(p^k)\}$ with an explicit criterion --- a lifting-the-exponent statement for the spine --- would complete the rank theory.

\textbf{Distribution of $\rank(p)$.} For which primes is $\rank(p)$ maximal, i.e.\ equal to $p \pm 1$? This is the Pell analogue of an Artin-type question about the order of $\delta$ in the residue field.

\textbf{Accident detection as a method.} The clustering at $P_7$ suggests a general algorithm: for a given linear recurrence, first locate all $n \le N$ at which $a_n$ has an unexpected factorisation, then test whole families of conjectures against those indices only. Making ``unexpected'' precise --- presumably via the expected size of the squarefull part --- would turn the observation into a tool.

\section{Conclusion}

The Pell spine, generated by the silver unit $1+\sqrt2$, carries a complete and rigid divisibility theory: strong divisibility on the norm strand, a parity-graded law on the trace strand, an apparition theorem for every modulus, the exact law $m \mid P_n \iff \rank(m)\mid n$, multiplicativity of the rank on coprime moduli, and a Fermat law whose proof produces Euler's criterion as a by-product. It also carries a complete Diophantine classification --- the spine \emph{is} the unit group of $\Z[\sqrt2]$, and its odd part \emph{is} the set of near-isosceles Pythagorean triples --- together with an exact approximation identity for $\sqrt2$.

Around this rigid core lie seven natural strengthenings, all false, all within the first thirty terms, clustering around a single arithmetic accident $P_7 = 169 = 13^2$ which also makes $13$ a Wall--Sun--Sun-type prime. The second such prime, $31$, follows quickly. Where the golden-ratio analogue has yielded nothing to searches out to seventeen digits, the silver ratio hands over two examples below $50$ --- and, we suspect, infinitely many more.

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt, lcm
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Optional, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The two strands of the spine
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def pell_P(n: int) -> int:
    """Pell number P(n): P(0)=0, P(1)=1, P(n+2)=2P(n+1)+P(n)."""
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, 2 * b + a
    return a


def pell_Q(n: int) -> int:
    """Half-companion Pell number Q(n): Q(0)=Q(1)=1, Q(n+2)=2Q(n+1)+Q(n)."""
    a, b = 1, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, 2 * b + a
    return a


def pell_pair(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (Q(n), P(n)), i.e. the coordinates of (1+sqrt 2)^n in Z[sqrt 2]."""
    return pell_Q(n), pell_P(n)


def pell_P_mod(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """P(n) mod m, computed without ever forming the (huge) integer P(n)."""
    if m == 1:
        return 0
    a, b = 0 % m, 1 % m
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, (2 * b + a) % m
    return a


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Rank of apparition
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def pell_rank(m: int, bound: Optional[int] = None) -> int:
    """Rank of apparition of m: least n > 0 with m | P(n).

    The apparition theorem guarantees this exists for every m >= 1; the search is
    bounded a priori by m^2 (the number of states (P(n), P(n+1)) mod m).
    """
    if m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("modulus must be positive")
    if bound is None:
        bound = m * m + 1
    a, b = 0, 1 % m
    for n in range(1, bound + 1):
        a, b = b, (2 * b + a) % m
        if a == 0:
            return n
    raise RuntimeError(f"no rank found for m={m} below {bound}")


def pell_period(m: int) -> int:
    """Pisano-style period: least t > 0 with (P(t), P(t+1)) = (P(0), P(1)) mod m."""
    if m == 1:
        return 1
    a, b = 0, 1 % m
    for t in range(1, m * m + 2):
        a, b = b, (2 * b + a) % m
        if (a, b) == (0, 1 % m):
            return t
    raise RuntimeError("period not found")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Utility predicates
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 2
    return True


def is_square(n: int) -> bool:
    return n >= 0 and isqrt(n) ** 2 == n


def is_squarefree(n: int) -> bool:
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % (d * d) == 0:
            return False
        d += 1
    return n >= 1


def legendre_two(p: int) -> int:
    """The Legendre symbol (2/p) for an odd prime p: +1 iff p = +-1 mod 8."""
    return 1 if p % 8 in (1, 7) else -1

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, isqrt, lcm
from typing import Dict, Iterator, List, Optional, Tuple

# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 1. The two strands of the spine
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def pell_P(n: int) -> int:
    """Pell number P(n): P(0)=0, P(1)=1, P(n+2)=2P(n+1)+P(n)."""
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, 2 * b + a
    return a


def pell_Q(n: int) -> int:
    """Half-companion Pell number Q(n): Q(0)=Q(1)=1, Q(n+2)=2Q(n+1)+Q(n)."""
    a, b = 1, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, 2 * b + a
    return a


def pell_pair(n: int) -> Tuple[int, int]:
    """Return (Q(n), P(n)), i.e. the coordinates of (1+sqrt 2)^n in Z[sqrt 2]."""
    return pell_Q(n), pell_P(n)


def pell_P_mod(n: int, m: int) -> int:
    """P(n) mod m, computed without ever forming the (huge) integer P(n)."""
    if m == 1:
        return 0
    a, b = 0 % m, 1 % m
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, (2 * b + a) % m
    return a


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Rank of apparition
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def pell_rank(m: int, bound: Optional[int] = None) -> int:
    """Rank of apparition of m: least n > 0 with m | P(n).

    The apparition theorem guarantees this exists for every m >= 1; the search is
    bounded a priori by m^2 (the number of states (P(n), P(n+1)) mod m).
    """
    if m <= 0:
        raise ValueError("modulus must be positive")
    if bound is None:
        bound = m * m + 1
    a, b = 0, 1 % m
    for n in range(1, bound + 1):
        a, b = b, (2 * b + a) % m
        if a == 0:
            return n
    raise RuntimeError(f"no rank found for m={m} below {bound}")


def pell_period(m: int) -> int:
    """Pisano-style period: least t > 0 with (P(t), P(t+1)) = (P(0), P(1)) mod m."""
    if m == 1:
        return 1
    a, b = 0, 1 % m
    for t in range(1, m * m + 2):
        a, b = b, (2 * b + a) % m
        if (a, b) == (0, 1 % m):
            return t
    raise RuntimeError("period not found")


# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Utility predicates
# ----------------------------------------------------------------------------


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 2:
        return False
    if n % 2 == 0:
        return n == 2
    d = 3
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 2
    return True


def is_square(n: int) -> bool:
    return n >= 0 and isqrt(n) ** 2 == n


def is_squarefree(n: int) -> bool:
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % (d * d) == 0:
            return False
        d += 1
    return n >= 1


def legendre_two(p: int) -> int:
    """The Legendre symbol (2/p) for an odd prime p: +1 iff p = +-1 mod 8."""
    return 1 if p % 8 in (1, 7) else -1

            out[d] = out.get(d, 0) + 1
            n //= d
        d += 1 if d == 2 else 2

    return 3 * x + 4 * y, 2 * x + 3 * y

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd, log
from typing import List

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import numpy as np


def pell_P(n: int) -> int:
    a, b = 0, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, 2 * b + a
    return a


def pell_Q(n: int) -> int:
    a, b = 1, 1
    for _ in range(n):
        a, b = b, 2 * b + a
    return a


def pell_rank(m: int) -> int:
    a, b = 0, 1 % m
    for n in range(1, m * m + 2):
        a, b = b, (2 * b + a) % m
        if a == 0:
            return n
    raise RuntimeError("unreachable: apparition theorem guarantees a rank")


def is_prime(n: int) -> bool:
    if n < 2:
        return False
    d = 2
    while d * d <= n:
        if n % d == 0:
            return False
        d += 1
    return True


def wall_sun_sun(bound: int) -> List[int]:
    out: List[int] = []
    for p in range(3, bound + 1):
        if not is_prime(p):
            continue
        r = pell_rank(p)
        a, b = 0, 1 % (p * p)
        for _ in range(r):
            a, b = b, (2 * b + a) % (p * p)
        if a == 0:
            out.append(p)
    return out

                 "a perfect divisor lattice")
    ax.set_xlabel("$n$")
    ax.set_ylabel("$m$")
    fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.046)

    # ---- Panel C: parity grading for Q ------------------------------------
    ax = axes[1][0]
    grid2 = np.zeros((N, N))
    for m in range(1, N + 1):
        for n in range(1, N + 1):
            g = gcd(m, n)
            both_odd = (m // g) % 2 == 1 and (n // g) % 2 == 1
            grid2[m - 1][n - 1] = log(pell_Q(g) + 1) if both_odd else 0.0

    ax.set_title("C. $\\gcd(Q_m,Q_n)$: equals $Q_{\\gcd(m,n)}$ only when both\n"

/* ---------- arithmetic core (BigInt where the numbers get large) ---------- */
function pellPair(n){            // (Q_n, P_n) as BigInt
  let q=1n,p=0n;
  for(let i=0;i<n;i++){ const np=p+q, nq=q+2n*p; p=np; q=nq; }
  return [q,p];
}
function P(n){ return pellPair(n)[1]; }
function Q(n){ return pellPair(n)[0]; }
function bgcd(a,b){ a=a<0n?-a:a; b=b<0n?-b:b; while(b){ [a,b]=[b,a%b]; } return a; }
function gcd(a,b){ while(b){ [a,b]=[b,a%b]; } return a; }
function lcm(a,b){ return a/gcd(a,b)*b; }
function pellPmod(n,m){          // P_n mod m with small numbers only
  if(m===1) return 0;
  let a=0,b=1%m;
  for(let i=0;i<n;i++){ const t=(2*b+a)%m; a=b; b=t; }
  return a;
}
function pellPairModFast(n,m){   // (P_n, Q_n) mod m by doubling, O(log n)
  if(m===1) return [0,0];
  if(n===0) return [0,1%m];
  const [p,q]=pellPairModFast(Math.floor(n/2),m);
  const p2=(2*p*q)%m, q2=(q*q+2*p*p)%m;
  return (n%2===0)?[p2,q2]:[(p2+q2)%m,(q2+2*p2)%m];
}
function pellPairModBig(n,m){    // (P_n, Q_n) mod m with BigInt safety
  const M=BigInt(m);
  if(M===1n) return [0n,0n];
  if(n===0) return [0n,1n%M];
  const [p,q]=pellPairModBig(Math.floor(n/2),m);
  const p2=(2n*p*q)%M, q2=(q*q+2n*p*p)%M;
  return (n%2===0)?[p2,q2]:[(p2+q2)%M,(q2+2n*p2)%M];
}
function isPrime(n){ if(n<2) return false; for(let d=2;d*d<=n;d++) if(n%d===0) return false; return true; }
function divisors(n){ const s=[],l=[]; for(let d=1;d*d<=n;d++) if(n%d===0){ s.push(d); if(d!==n/d) l.push(n/d);} return s.concat(l.reverse()); }
function legendreTwo(p){ const r=p%8; return (r===1||r===7)?1:-1; }
function rankPrime(p){ if(p===2) return 2; for(const d of divisors(p-legendreTwo(p))) if(pellPairModFast(d,p)[0]===0) return d; return -1; }
function pellRank(m){            // brute force, fine for the ranges here
  if(m<1) return 0;
  let a=0,b=1%m;
  for(let n=1;n<=m*m+1;n++){ const t=(2*b+a)%m; a=b; b=t; if(a===0) return n; }
  return -1;
}
function fmt(b){ return b.toString().replace(/\B(?=(\d{3})+(?!\d))/g,"\u2009"); }

## 1. Where we are going

Almost everyone meets the Fibonacci numbers. Far fewer meet their close relative, born from a rule that is barely different:

$$P_0 = 0,\qquad P_1 = 1,\qquad P_{n+2} = 2P_{n+1} + P_n.$$

$$0,\ 1,\ 2,\ 5,\ 12,\ 29,\ 70,\ \mathbf{169},\ 408,\ 985,\ 2378,\ \dots$$

These are the **Pell numbers**. By the end of this page you will know:

* why they are the shadow of the number $1+\sqrt2$, the *silver ratio*;
* the exact law that decides which Pell number a given integer divides;
* why their companion sequence obeys a *different* law, graded by parity;
* and why the eighth entry, $169 = 13^2$, is a demolition charge that destroys five plausible conjectures simultaneously — and turns the prime $13$ into an object that number theorists have hunted unsuccessfully in the Fibonacci world for decades.

Nothing below assumes more than school algebra and a willingness to compute.

---

## 2. The silver ratio and its integer shadow

Raise $1+\sqrt2$ to a power and something tidy happens. Because $(\sqrt2)^2 = 2$ is an integer, every power collapses to the form $q + p\sqrt2$ with $p,q$ whole:

$$(1+\sqrt2)^1 = 1 + 1\sqrt2,\qquad (1+\sqrt2)^2 = 3 + 2\sqrt2,\qquad (1+\sqrt2)^3 = 7 + 5\sqrt2,\qquad (1+\sqrt2)^4 = 17 + 12\sqrt2 .$$

The $\sqrt2$-coefficients $1,2,5,12,\dots$ are the Pell numbers. The rational parts $1,3,7,17,\dots$ form the **half-companion** sequence $Q$, obeying the identical recursion from the seed $Q_0 = Q_1 = 1$. In one line:

$$\boxed{(1+\sqrt2)^n = Q_n + P_n\sqrt2}$$

Call the interleaved pair $(Q_n, P_n)$ the **Pell spine**.

Multiply this by its mirror image $(1-\sqrt2)^n = Q_n - P_n\sqrt2$. Since $(1+\sqrt2)(1-\sqrt2) = 1 - 2 = -1$, we get the identity that runs the whole show:

$$Q_n^2 - 2P_n^2 = (-1)^n .$$

Try it: $3^2 - 2\cdot 2^2 = 1$, $7^2 - 2\cdot 5^2 = -1$, $17^2 - 2\cdot 12^2 = 1$. That alternating sign will turn out to be the hidden variable behind almost everything else on this page — including which side of $\sqrt2$ the fraction $Q_n/P_n$ lies on, and which pairs of companion numbers share a factor.

**Explore the spine yourself.** Open the first tab of the widget below and watch the norm column: always $\pm1$, always alternating. Then come back.

{{interactive_demo:0}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: why the two strands satisfy the same recursion</b></summary>

Multiplying $q + p\sqrt2$ by $1+\sqrt2$ gives $(q + 2p) + (p+q)\sqrt2$. So the one-step laws are

$$P_{n+1} = P_n + Q_n, \qquad Q_{n+1} = Q_n + 2P_n .$$

Apply the first twice and substitute: $P_{n+2} = P_{n+1} + Q_{n+1} = P_{n+1} + Q_n + 2P_n = P_{n+1} + (P_{n+1} - P_n) + 2P_n = 2P_{n+1} + P_n$. The same computation works for $Q$. Both strands inherit the recursion from the single fact that $1+\sqrt2$ satisfies $x^2 = 2x+1$.

More generally, multiplying $\delta^m$ by $\delta^n$ gives the **addition laws**

$$P_{m+n} = P_mQ_n + Q_mP_n, \qquad Q_{m+n} = Q_mQ_n + 2P_mP_n,$$

which are the workhorses of every proof below.
</details>

## 3. The law of divisibility

Here is the deepest fact about the Pell numbers.

> **Strong Divisibility Theorem.** $\gcd(P_m, P_n) = P_{\gcd(m,n)}$ for all $m,n$.

The greatest common divisor of two Pell numbers is the Pell number of the greatest common divisor of their *indices*. As a consequence, $m \mid n$ exactly when $P_m \mid P_n$: divisibility of positions is mirrored perfectly in divisibility of values.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof — it is the Euclidean algorithm in disguise</b></summary>

Use the addition law $P_{m+n} = P_mQ_n + P_nQ_m$. The second term is a multiple of $P_n$, so modulo $P_n$ we have $P_{m+n} \equiv P_mQ_n$. Now, $Q_n$ is coprime to $P_n$: any common factor would divide $Q_n^2 - 2P_n^2 = \pm1$. A factor coprime to $P_n$ cannot contribute to a gcd with $P_n$, so

$$\gcd(P_{m+n}, P_n) = \gcd(P_m, P_n).$$

That is one step of the Euclidean algorithm, performed on the indices. Iterating it replaces $(m,n)$ by $(n, m \bmod n)$, exactly as Euclid does, and the process terminates at $\gcd(P_0, P_g) = P_g$ where $g = \gcd(m,n)$. $\blacksquare$
</details>

Now switch the widget above to its second tab, **Divisibility lattices**, and look at the picture for the $P$ strand. It is a perfect divisor lattice: bright wherever the indices share a large factor. Then flip the radio button to the companion strand $Q$ — and watch the lattice get punched full of holes.

That is not a rendering bug. It is a theorem.

## 4. Where the companion strand breaks — and what replaces it

The two strands satisfy the same recursion, so surely they satisfy the same divisibility law? They do not. Take $m=3$, $n=6$. Then $3 \mid 6$, so we would expect $Q_3 = 7$ to divide $Q_6 = 99$. It does not — and worse, $\gcd(7,99) = 1$, the smallest value possible.

The correct statement grades everything by **parity**:

> **Companion Divisibility Law.** For $m \geq 2$: $\ Q_m \mid Q_n$ if and only if $n = mk$ with $k$ **odd**.
>
> **Companion GCD Law.** With $g = \gcd(m,n)$,
> $$\gcd(Q_m, Q_n) = \begin{cases} Q_g & \text{if } m/g \text{ and } n/g \text{ are both odd},\\ 1 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$

Odd multiples work; even multiples never do. $Q_3 = 7$ divides $Q_9 = 1393$ and $Q_{15} = 275807$, but shares no factor at all with $Q_6$ or $Q_{12}$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: why even multiples are impossible</b></summary>

Work modulo $Q_m$. The addition law gives $Q_{a+2m} = Q_aQ_{2m} + 2P_aP_{2m}$. Two facts kill the second term and simplify the first: $P_{2m} = 2P_mQ_m$ is a multiple of $Q_m$, and $Q_{2m} = Q_m^2 + 2P_m^2 \equiv 2P_m^2$. So modulo $Q_m$,

$$Q_{a+2m} \equiv 2P_m^2 \, Q_a .$$

Starting from $Q_0 = 1$ and iterating $j$ times,

$$Q_{2jm} \equiv (2P_m^2)^j \pmod{Q_m}.$$

Every half-companion Pell number is odd, and $Q_m$ is coprime to $P_m$, so $2P_m^2$ is *invertible* modulo $Q_m$. Its powers are never $0$. Therefore $Q_m$ can never divide $Q_{2jm}$: even multiples are permanently excluded, no matter how far out you look. $\blacksquare$
</details>

The moral is worth stating plainly: **strong divisibility is a property of the norm-form strand $P$, not of the trace strand $Q$; on $Q$ it does not disappear, it becomes graded by parity.** And the grading traces straight back to the alternating sign $(-1)^n$ in $Q_n^2 - 2P_n^2$.

---

## 5. Every number appears — the rank of apparition

Pick any whole number $m$. Does it divide *some* Pell number? It is far from obvious. But the answer is always yes, and the proof is a small gem.

> **Apparition Theorem.** Every $m \geq 1$ divides some positive Pell number.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the pigeonhole proof</b></summary>

Track the pair $(P_n, P_{n+1})$ modulo $m$. There are only $m^2$ possible pairs, so as $n$ runs over all of $\mathbb{N}$ some pair must recur: $(P_i, P_{i+1}) \equiv (P_j, P_{j+1})$ with $i<j$.

Now the crucial observation: the recursion can be run **backwards**, since $P_n = P_{n+2} - 2P_{n+1}$. So if two consecutive-pairs agree at positions $i+1$ and $j+1$, they also agree at $i$ and $j$. Rewind the repetition step by step until the left-hand index reaches zero:

$$(P_0, P_1) \equiv (P_t, P_{t+1}) \pmod m, \qquad t = j-i > 0.$$

But $P_0 = 0$. Hence $m \mid P_t$. $\blacksquare$

The argument uses no primality, no factorisation, no advanced algebra — just finiteness plus the fact that the transition matrix $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}2&1\\1&0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ has determinant $-1$ and is therefore invertible modulo every $m$.
</details>

Define the **rank of apparition** $\alpha(m)$ to be the least $n>0$ with $m \mid P_n$. Then the two theorems above combine into something much stronger than either:

> **Divisibility Law.** $m \mid P_n$ **if and only if** $\alpha(m) \mid n$.

The set of indices where $m$ appears is exactly the multiples of the first one. Nothing is skipped; nothing extra sneaks in.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the two-line proof, where pigeonhole meets Euclid</b></summary>

Suppose $m \mid P_n$. We also know $m \mid P_{\alpha(m)}$, so $m$ divides $\gcd(P_{\alpha(m)}, P_n)$, which strong divisibility identifies as $P_{\gcd(\alpha(m),\,n)}$. So $m$ appears at index $\gcd(\alpha(m),n)$ — but $\alpha(m)$ was defined to be the *smallest* index where $m$ appears, and a gcd cannot exceed either argument. Minimality forces $\gcd(\alpha(m),n) = \alpha(m)$, i.e. $\alpha(m) \mid n$. The converse is immediate. $\blacksquare$

A consequence worth noting: for coprime $a,b$, $\ \alpha(ab) = \operatorname{lcm}(\alpha(a),\alpha(b))$. So the whole rank function is determined by its values on prime powers.
</details>

## 6. A Fermat law, and why the naive guess fails

For most sequences of this kind there is a Fermat-style law. The obvious guess is $p \mid P_{p-1}$ for odd primes $p$. Test it at $p=3$: is $3 \mid P_2 = 2$? No. Guess dead, at the first opportunity.

The truth is a dichotomy:

> **Fermat Law.** For every odd prime $p$: $\ p \mid P_{p-1}P_{p+1}$; equivalently $\alpha(p)$ divides $p-1$ **or** $\alpha(p)$ divides $p+1$.

Which of the two is decided by whether $2$ is a square modulo $p$ — that is, by whether $p \equiv \pm1 \pmod 8$.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal the proof: Euler's criterion falls out of the freshman's dream</b></summary>

Work in the number system $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$ of expressions $a + b\sqrt2$ with $a,b$ integers. For any prime $p$, all the middle binomial coefficients $\binom{p}{k}$ ($0<k<p$) are divisible by $p$, so in any commutative ring

$$(x+y)^p = x^p + y^p + p\,xy\,r$$

for some ring element $r$ — the "freshman's dream", true after all, modulo $p$. Take $x = 1$, $y = \sqrt2$. Writing $p = 2m+1$ and using $(\sqrt2)^{2m+1} = 2^m\sqrt2$:

$$(1+\sqrt2)^p = 1 + 2^m\sqrt2 + p\sqrt2\,r .$$

The left-hand side is $Q_p + P_p\sqrt2$. Comparing $\sqrt2$-coefficients:

$$P_p \equiv 2^{(p-1)/2} \pmod p .$$

This is **Euler's criterion**, appearing spontaneously on the spine: the right-hand side is $+1$ or $-1$ according to whether $2$ is a quadratic residue mod $p$. Squaring and using Fermat's little theorem, $P_p^2 \equiv 2^{p-1} \equiv 1 \pmod p$. Finally, the Cassini-type identity $P_{p-1}P_{p+1} = P_p^2 - 1$ (valid for odd $p$) shows $p \mid P_{p-1}P_{p+1}$. Since $p$ is prime, it divides one of the two factors. $\blacksquare$

Back to the counterexample: for $p=3$, $\alpha(3) = 4$, and $4 \nmid 2$ but $4 \mid 4 = p+1$. The "failure" was the theorem showing its second face, exactly as the Legendre symbol predicts, since $2$ is a non-residue modulo $3$.
</details>

The `Fermat law` column in the rank tab checks this prediction for whichever prime you type in.

## 7. The prime 13, and a rarity that isn't rare

We now come to the strangest thing on this page.

For Fibonacci numbers, define the rank of apparition the same way. When you pass from a prime $p$ to $p^2$, the rank *generically* multiplies by $p$. A prime for which this fails — one with $p^2 \mid F_{\alpha_F(p)}$ — is called a [Wall–Sun–Sun prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wall%E2%80%93Sun%E2%80%93Sun_prime). They were once tied to the first case of [Fermat's Last Theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_Last_Theorem), and despite decades of computation, **not a single one is known** — none below $10^{17}$.

Run the same test on the Pell spine. Recall $P_7 = 169 = 13^2$. Since $\alpha(13) = 7$ and $13^2$ already divides $P_7$, we get $\alpha(169) = 7$ too — not $7 \times 13 = 91$. The growth law fails at the very first interesting prime.

And it is not a one-off. The next one is close by:

$$31^2 \mid P_{30} = 107\,578\,520\,350, \qquad \alpha(31) = \alpha(961) = 30 .$$

Two exceptional primes below $50$, in a setting where the golden-ratio analogue has produced none in seventeen digits.

Try it: open the widget's fourth tab, **Wall–Sun–Sun hunter**, and search up to $20\,000$. You will get exactly two hits.

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: is this luck, or structure?</b></summary>

The standard heuristic treats $P_{\alpha(p)}/p \bmod p$ as uniformly random in $\{0,1,\dots,p-1\}$, so $p$ is exceptional with probability about $1/p$. Summing $1/p$ over primes gives a counting function of order $\log\log x$ — growth so slow that finding *nothing* below $10^{17}$ is entirely unsurprising.

The Pell setting has an extra feature: the relevant discriminant is $8$, so the prime $2$ is **ramified**, whereas in the Fibonacci setting (discriminant $5$) it is not. Heuristically this doubles the density constant. Two hits below $10^2$ is still small-numbers territory, but it is consistent with a doubled constant — and it makes the silver ratio a far more tractable laboratory for a phenomenon that is essentially invisible in the golden one.

**Open conjecture.** The set of Pell–Wall–Sun–Sun primes is infinite, with counting function asymptotic to $c\log\log x$, and $13, 31$ are its first two members.
</details>

## 8. The same number, five times over

Something curious happens when you catalogue the counterexamples. Consider five natural conjectures, from four different areas of mathematics:

| Conjecture | Verdict |
|---|---|
| A prime index gives a prime Pell number | **false** |
| Every Pell number is squarefree | **false** |
| No Pell number past the first is a perfect square | **false** |
| The hypotenuse of a near-isosceles right triangle is prime | **false** |
| Passing from $p$ to $p^2$ multiplies the rank by $p$ | **false** |

Every one of them dies at the *same* term: $P_7 = 169 = 13^2$.

That last row, the geometric one, deserves a look of its own. A Pythagorean triple is **near-isosceles** if its legs are consecutive integers. Completing the square, $a^2 + (a+1)^2 = c^2$ becomes $(2a+1)^2 + 1 = 2c^2$ — the negative Pell equation. So these triples are *exactly* the odd-index points of the spine:

$$(3,4,5),\quad (20,21,29),\quad (119,120,169),\quad (696,697,985),\quad (4059,4060,5741),\ \dots$$

with $2a+1 = Q_{2k+1}$ and hypotenuse $c = P_{2k+1}$, and every hypotenuse congruent to $1$ modulo $4$. The fourth entry has hypotenuse $169 = 13^2$: a statement about triangles, felled by an arithmetic accident in a recurrence.

Switch to the fifth widget tab, **Near-isosceles triangles**, to see the list and the primality column.

The generation of these triples, and the descent that proves the classification, is itself a clean algorithm — a *decision procedure with certificate*, running in $O(\log y)$ steps rather than searching:

{{algorithm:2}}

<details>
<summary><b>Click to reveal: the descent, and the classification of $x^2-2y^2 = \pm1$</b></summary>

Multiplication by $3 - 2\sqrt2 = (1+\sqrt2)^{-2}$ sends $(x,y) \mapsto (3x-4y,\, 3y-2x)$ and preserves the value of $x^2 - 2y^2$. One checks that if $y \geq 2$ then the new $y$ is strictly smaller and still non-negative. So iterating must terminate — and the only places it can stop are $(1,0)$ and $(1,1)$. Climbing back up by $(x,y)\mapsto(3x+4y,\,2x+3y)$ retraces the spine two indices at a time.

Hence: **the non-negative solutions of $x^2 - 2y^2 = \pm 1$ are exactly the spine points $(Q_n, P_n)$**, with the sign of the norm equal to $(-1)^n$. This is Dirichlet's unit theorem for $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt2]$, made completely explicit.

Two more small facts round out the picture: $x^2 = 2y^2 + 3$ has *no* solutions (look modulo $8$: squares are $0,1,4$, but $2y^2+3$ is $3$ or $5$), whereas $x^2 - 2y^2 = 7$ does, via $3^2 - 2\cdot1^2$. So the values represented by the form are cut out by congruences, not by size.
</details>

## 9. Seeing it all at once

The following figure puts the four faces of the spine side by side: the erratic scatter of ranks with the two exceptional primes circled; the pristine divisor lattice of the $P$ strand; the same lattice, parity-punctured, for $Q$; and the geometric, side-alternating approximation of $\sqrt2$.

{{visualization:0}}

The bottom-right panel deserves a comment. Because $(1-\sqrt2)^n = Q_n - P_n\sqrt2$ and $|1-\sqrt2| = 0.41421\dots < 1$, we have the **exact** error formula

$$\bigl|Q_n - P_n\sqrt2\bigr| = (\sqrt2-1)^n,$$

from which $\left|\sqrt2 - Q_n/P_n\right| < 1/P_n^2$ for every $n \geq 1$: each convergent is accurate to roughly the square of its denominator, the gold standard for a rational approximation. The colours alternate because the sign of $Q_n - P_n\sqrt2$ is $(-1)^n$ — parity again.

Two tempting strengthenings fail. The constant cannot be improved to $1/3$: at $n=1$ the fraction is $1/1$ and the error is $0.414\ldots$. And the convergents do not approach from one side: $1 < \sqrt2 < 3/2$.

    rw [pow_succ, pow_mul]
    norm_num
  rw [hodd] at h
  have : ((pellQ (2 * k + 1) ^ 2 + 1 : ℕ) : ℤ) = ((2 * pellP (2 * k + 1) ^ 2 : ℕ) : ℤ) := by
    push_cast
    linarith
  exact_mod_cast this

theorem negPell_iff (x y : ℕ) :
    x ^ 2 + 1 = 2 * y ^ 2 ↔ ∃ k, x = pellQ (2 * k + 1) ∧ y = pellP (2 * k + 1) := by
  refine ⟨negPell_descent y x, ?_⟩
  rintro ⟨k, rfl, rfl⟩
  exact negPell_of_odd_index k

/-! ## Near-isosceles Pythagorean triples -/

/-- **Classification of near-isosceles Pythagorean triples.**  A triple with legs
`a, a+1` and hypotenuse `c` exists exactly at the odd points of the Pell spine. -/
theorem nearIsosceles_iff (a c : ℕ) :
    a ^ 2 + (a + 1) ^ 2 = c ^ 2 ↔
      ∃ k, 2 * a + 1 = pellQ (2 * k + 1) ∧ c = pellP (2 * k + 1) := by
  constructor
  · intro h
    have h' : (2 * a + 1) ^ 2 + 1 = 2 * c ^ 2 := by ring_nf; ring_nf at h; omega
    exact negPell_descent c (2 * a + 1) h'
  · rintro ⟨k, hq, rfl⟩
    have h := negPell_of_odd_index k
    rw [← hq] at h
    nlinarith [h]

/-- The classified triples are Pythagorean in the catalog's `IsPythag` sense. -/
theorem nearIsosceles_isPythag (k a : ℕ) (ha : 2 * a + 1 = pellQ (2 * k + 1)) :
    IsPythag (a : ℤ) ((a : ℤ) + 1) ((pellP (2 * k + 1) : ℕ) : ℤ) := by

  have : ((a ^ 2 + (a + 1) ^ 2 : ℕ) : ℤ) = ((pellP (2 * k + 1) ^ 2 : ℕ) : ℤ) := by
    exact_mod_cast h
  unfold IsPythag
  push_cast at this ⊢
  linarith

/-- Every leg pair really occurs: the odd companion terms are odd. -/
theorem exists_nearIsosceles (k : ℕ) :
    ∃ a : ℕ, 2 * a + 1 = pellQ (2 * k + 1) ∧ a ^ 2 + (a + 1) ^ 2 = pellP (2 * k + 1) ^ 2 := by
  have h := negPell_of_odd_index k
  have hodd : pellQ (2 * k + 1) % 2 = 1 := by

/-! ## An arithmetic constraint on the hypotenuse -/

/-- Three-term recursion for the Pell spine: `P (n+4) + P n = 6 * P (n+2)`. -/
theorem pellP_six_step (n : ℕ) : pellP (n + 4) + pellP n = 6 * pellP (n + 2) := by
  have h1 : pellP (n + 4) = 2 * pellP (n + 3) + pellP (n + 2) := pellP_add_two (n + 2)

  have h3 : pellP (n + 2) = 2 * pellP (n + 1) + pellP n := pellP_add_two n

      have e2 : 2 * (k + 1) + 1 = 2 * k + 1 + 2 := by ring
      rw [e2] at ih2
      rw [e1]
      omega

namespace Catalog.Novelty.PellSpine

/-! ## The spine inside `ℤ[√2]` -/

/-- The silver unit `1 + √2` inside `ℤ[√2]` generates the spine:
`(1 + √2)ⁿ = ⟨Q n, P n⟩`. -/
theorem silver_zsqrtd_pow (n : ℕ) :
    ((1 : Zsqrtd 2) + Zsqrtd.sqrtd) ^ n = ⟨(pellQ n : ℤ), (pellP n : ℤ)⟩ := by
  induction n with
  | zero => rfl
  | succ n ih =>
      rw [pow_succ, ih]
      refine Zsqrtd.ext ?_ ?_
      · have h : pellQ (n + 1) = pellQ n + 2 * pellP n := pellQ_succ n
        simp [Zsqrtd.re_mul, h]
      · have h : pellP (n + 1) = pellP n + pellQ n := pellP_succ n
        simp [Zsqrtd.im_mul, h]
        ring

/-- Odd powers of `√2`: `(√2)^(2m+1) = 2^m √2`. -/
theorem sqrtd_pow_odd (m : ℕ) :
    (Zsqrtd.sqrtd : Zsqrtd 2) ^ (2 * m + 1) = ⟨0, 2 ^ m⟩ := by
  induction m with
  | zero => refine Zsqrtd.ext ?_ ?_ <;> simp
  | succ m ih =>
      have hidx : 2 * (m + 1) + 1 = (2 * m + 1) + 2 := by ring
      rw [hidx, pow_add, ih]
      refine Zsqrtd.ext ?_ ?_ <;> simp [Zsqrtd.re_mul, Zsqrtd.im_mul, pow_succ]

/-! ## Euler's criterion on the spine -/

/-- **Frobenius on the spine.**  For an odd prime `p = 2m+1`,
`P p ≡ 2^m` and `Q p ≡ 1` modulo `p`.  The first congruence *is* Euler's criterion for `2`. -/
theorem pell_frobenius {p : ℕ} (hp : Nat.Prime p) {m : ℕ} (hm : p = 2 * m + 1) :
    ((pellP p : ℕ) : ZMod p) = (2 : ZMod p) ^ m ∧ ((pellQ p : ℕ) : ZMod p) = 1 := by
  subst hm
  obtain ⟨r, hr⟩ := exists_add_pow_prime_eq hp (1 : Zsqrtd 2) Zsqrtd.sqrtd
  rw [silver_zsqrtd_pow (2 * m + 1), one_pow, sqrtd_pow_odd m] at hr
  have hp0 : (2 * (m : ZMod (2 * m + 1)) + 1) = 0 := by
    have h1 : ((2 * m + 1 : ℕ) : ZMod (2 * m + 1)) = 0 := ZMod.natCast_self _
    push_cast at h1
    exact h1
  constructor
  · have him := congrArg Zsqrtd.im hr
    simp [Zsqrtd.im_mul, Zsqrtd.re_mul] at him
    have hz := congrArg (fun z : ℤ => (z : ZMod (2 * m + 1))) him
    push_cast at hz
    rw [hz, hp0]
    ring
  · have hre := congrArg Zsqrtd.re hr
    simp [Zsqrtd.im_mul, Zsqrtd.re_mul] at hre
    have hz := congrArg (fun z : ℤ => (z : ZMod (2 * m + 1))) hre
    push_cast at hz
    rw [hz, hp0]
    ring

/-- **`P p ≡ 2^((p-1)/2) (mod p)`** for odd primes `p`: the Legendre symbol of `2` shows up
as the `p`-th Pell number. -/
theorem pellP_prime_congr {p : ℕ} (hp : Nat.Prime p) {m : ℕ} (hm : p = 2 * m + 1) :
    ((pellP p : ℕ) : ZMod p) = (2 : ZMod p) ^ m := (pell_frobenius hp hm).1

/-- The companion sequence satisfies `Q p ≡ 1 (mod p)`. -/
theorem pellQ_prime_congr {p : ℕ} (hp : Nat.Prime p) {m : ℕ} (hm : p = 2 * m + 1) :
    ((pellQ p : ℕ) : ZMod p) = 1 := (pell_frobenius hp hm).2

/-- Squaring Euler's criterion and applying Fermat's little theorem: `P p ² ≡ 1 (mod p)`. -/
theorem pellP_prime_sq_congr {p : ℕ} (hp : Nat.Prime p) (hodd : p ≠ 2) :
    (((pellP p : ℕ) : ZMod p)) ^ 2 = 1 := by
  haveI : Fact (Nat.Prime p) := ⟨hp⟩
  obtain ⟨m, hm⟩ : ∃ m, p = 2 * m + 1 := by
    rcases hp.eq_two_or_odd' with h | h
    · exact absurd h hodd
    · obtain ⟨k, hk⟩ := h; exact ⟨k, by omega⟩
  rw [pellP_prime_congr hp hm, ← pow_mul]
  have h2 : (2 : ZMod p) ≠ 0 := by
    intro h
    have hdvd : p ∣ 2 := (ZMod.natCast_eq_zero_iff (2 : ℕ) p).mp (by exact_mod_cast h)
    exact hodd ((Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq hp Nat.prime_two).mp hdvd)
  have : m * 2 = p - 1 := by omega
  rw [this]
  exact ZMod.pow_card_sub_one_eq_one h2

/-! ## The Fermat law -/

/-- **The Fermat law of the Pell spine**: every odd prime divides `P (p-1) · P (p+1)`.
The naive `p ∣ P (p-1)` (refuted at `p = 3`) is only the `(2/p) = 1` half of this. -/
theorem pell_fermat_law {p : ℕ} (hp : Nat.Prime p) (hodd : p ≠ 2) :
    p ∣ pellP (p - 1) * pellP (p + 1) := by
  haveI : Fact (Nat.Prime p) := ⟨hp⟩
  have hppos : 0 < p := hp.pos
  obtain ⟨n, hn⟩ : ∃ n, p = n + 1 := ⟨p - 1, by omega⟩
  have hp1 : p - 1 = n := by omega
  -- `Q p = P p + P (p-1)` and `P (p+1) = P p + Q p`
  have hQ : pellQ p = pellP p + pellP n := by rw [hn]; exact pellQ_succ_eq_add n
  have hP1 : pellP (p + 1) = pellP p + pellQ p := pellP_succ p
  -- the Pell equation at the odd index `p`
  have hpe : ((pellQ p : ℤ)) ^ 2 - 2 * ((pellP p : ℤ)) ^ 2 = -1 := by
    have h := pell_equation p
    have : ((-1 : ℤ)) ^ p = -1 := by
      rcases hp.eq_two_or_odd' with h2 | h2
      · exact absurd h2 hodd
      · exact Odd.neg_one_pow h2
    rw [this] at h
    exact h

  have hgoal : (((pellP (p - 1) * pellP (p + 1) : ℕ)) : ZMod p) = 0 := by
    have hsq := pellP_prime_sq_congr hp hodd

      exact_mod_cast congrArg (fun k : ℕ => (k : ZMod p)) hQ
    have hP1z : ((pellP (p + 1) : ℕ) : ZMod p)
        = ((pellP p : ℕ) : ZMod p) + ((pellQ p : ℕ) : ZMod p) := by
      exact_mod_cast congrArg (fun k : ℕ => (k : ZMod p)) hP1
    have hpez : ((pellQ p : ℕ) : ZMod p) ^ 2 - 2 * ((pellP p : ℕ) : ZMod p) ^ 2 = -1 := by
      have : (((pellQ p : ℤ)) ^ 2 - 2 * ((pellP p : ℤ)) ^ 2 : ℤ) = -1 := hpe
      have := congrArg (fun z : ℤ => (z : ZMod p)) this
      push_cast at this
      exact this
    push_cast [hp1, hP1z, hQz]

    have hPn : ((pellP n : ℕ) : ZMod p)

    push_cast at hsq ⊢
    linear_combination hpez + hsq

/-- Sharpened: an odd prime divides `P (p-1)` or `P (p+1)`. -/
theorem pell_fermat_law_or {p : ℕ} (hp : Nat.Prime p) (hodd : p ≠ 2) :

The *silver ratio* `1 + √2` is the fundamental unit of `ℤ[√2]`, and it already appears
throughout the catalog (`Novelty.BerggrenTreeCriticalLine.silverUnit`,
`Novelty.HyperbolicBerggrenSilverGrowth.silver`, `Shared.BerggrenTQC.SilverSpectrum`).

* `pellP` : `0, 1, 2, 5, 12, 29, 70, 169, 408, …`  (Pell numbers, OEIS A000129)
* `pellQ` : `1, 1, 3, 7, 17, 41, 99, 239, 577, …`  (half-companion Pell, OEIS A001333)

determined by `(1 + √2)ⁿ = pellQ n + pellP n · √2`.

* `pellP_add`, `pellQ_add` — the two addition laws, proved by a single simultaneous

/-- Pell numbers `0, 1, 2, 5, 12, 29, …`: `P (n+2) = 2 * P (n+1) + P n`. -/
def pellP : ℕ → ℕ
  | 0 => 0
  | 1 => 1
  | n + 2 => 2 * pellP (n + 1) + pellP n

@[simp] theorem pellQ_one : pellQ 1 = 1 := rfl

      · rw [pellQ_add_two, hP, hQ]; ring

# Ranks of apparition on the Pell spine, and the prime `13`

`Novelty.PellSpineDivisibility` shows that the Pell numbers are a strong divisibility
sequence.  Here we combine that with a pigeonhole argument in `ZMod m × ZMod m` to obtain
the *rank of apparition* theory, and then use it to falsify two more conjectures.

* `pell_apparition` — **every** modulus `m ≥ 1` divides some positive Pell number.  The

* `not_pellRank_dvd_sub_one` — the Fermat-style guess `pellRank p ∣ p - 1` fails at `p = 3`
  (`pellRank 3 = 4`, and `4 ∤ 2`); the correct exponent involves the Legendre symbol `(2/p)`;
* `not_pellRank_sq` — the Wall–Sun–Sun-style guess `pellRank (p²) = p * pellRank p` fails at

import Novelty.PellSpineDivisibility

namespace Catalog.Novelty.PellSpine

/-! ## Existence of the rank of apparition -/

/-- **Apparition theorem**: every positive modulus divides some positive Pell number.
Pigeonhole on the reversible state map `n ↦ (P n, P (n+1)) ∈ ZMod m × ZMod m`. -/
theorem pell_apparition (m : ℕ) (hm : 0 < m) : ∃ n, 0 < n ∧ m ∣ pellP n := by
  haveI : NeZero m := ⟨hm.ne'⟩
  set f : ℕ → ZMod m × ZMod m := fun n => ((pellP n : ZMod m), (pellP (n + 1) : ZMod m))
    with hf
  -- the recursion can be run backwards
  have hback : ∀ a b : ℕ, f (a + 1) = f (b + 1) → f a = f b := by
    intro a b h
    have h1 : ((pellP (a + 1) : ℕ) : ZMod m) = ((pellP (b + 1) : ℕ) : ZMod m) :=
      congrArg Prod.fst h
    have h2 : ((pellP (a + 2) : ℕ) : ZMod m) = ((pellP (b + 2) : ℕ) : ZMod m) :=
      congrArg Prod.snd h
    have e : ∀ n : ℕ, ((pellP (n + 2) : ℕ) : ZMod m)
        = 2 * ((pellP (n + 1) : ℕ) : ZMod m) + ((pellP n : ℕ) : ZMod m) := by
      intro n; rw [pellP_add_two]; push_cast; ring
    rw [e a, e b] at h2
    have h0 : ((pellP a : ℕ) : ZMod m) = ((pellP b : ℕ) : ZMod m) := by
      linear_combination h2 - 2 * h1
    exact Prod.ext h0 h1
  -- hence a repetition slides down to the origin
  have hshift : ∀ t i : ℕ, f i = f (i + t) → f 0 = f t := by
    intro t i
    induction i with
    | zero => simp
    | succ i ih =>
        intro h
        refine ih (hback i (i + t) ?_)
        rw [show i + t + 1 = i + 1 + t by ring]
        exact h
  have key : ∀ i j : ℕ, i < j → f i = f j → ∃ n, 0 < n ∧ m ∣ pellP n := by
    intro i j hij hfij
    obtain ⟨t, ht⟩ : ∃ t, j = i + t := ⟨j - i, by omega⟩

  rcases lt_or_gt_of_ne hab with h | h

  · exact key b a h hfab.symm

/-- The **rank of apparition** of `m`: the least positive index whose Pell number is
divisible by `m` (and `0` for the degenerate modulus `m = 0`). -/
noncomputable def pellRank (m : ℕ) : ℕ :=
  if h : 0 < m then Nat.find (pell_apparition m h) else 0

theorem pellRank_spec {m : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m) : 0 < pellRank m ∧ m ∣ pellP (pellRank m) := by
  rw [pellRank, dif_pos hm]
  exact Nat.find_spec (pell_apparition m hm)

theorem pellRank_pos {m : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m) : 0 < pellRank m := (pellRank_spec hm).1

theorem dvd_pellP_pellRank {m : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m) : m ∣ pellP (pellRank m) :=
  (pellRank_spec hm).2

theorem pellRank_le {m n : ℕ} (hm : 0 < m) (hn : 0 < n) (h : m ∣ pellP n) : pellRank m ≤ n := by
  rw [pellRank, dif_pos hm]
  exact Nat.find_le ⟨hn, h⟩

/-- **The divisibility law of the Pell spine**: `m ∣ P n` happens exactly at the multiples

    push_cast at this
    exact this

  intro h

  norm_num at this

      = if Odd (m / Nat.gcd m n) ∧ Odd (n / Nat.gcd m n) then pellQ (Nat.gcd m n) else 1 := by

/-! ## Refutations -/

theorem pellQ_two : pellQ 2 = 3 := by decide

theorem pellQ_four : pellQ 4 = 17 := by decide

/-- **Refutation.**  The companion sequence is not divisibility-closed along multiples:

theorem not_pellQ_dvd_all_multiples : ¬ ∀ n k : ℕ, pellQ n ∣ pellQ (k * n) := by
  intro h
  have h24 := h 2 2
  norm_num [pellQ_two, pellQ_four] at h24

theorem not_pellQ_dvd_iff_index_dvd : ¬ ∀ m n : ℕ, m ∣ n → pellQ m ∣ pellQ n := by
  intro h
  have h24 := h 2 4 ⟨2, rfl⟩
  norm_num [pellQ_two, pellQ_four] at h24

/-! ## Summation identities linking the two strands -/

/-- Partial sums of the half-companion sequence are Pell numbers. -/
theorem pellQ_sum (n : ℕ) : ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), pellQ i = pellP (n + 1) := by
  induction n with
  | zero => decide
  | succ k ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, ih, ← pellP_succ]

/-- Partial sums of the Pell sequence. -/
theorem pellP_sum (n : ℕ) :
    2 * ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), pellP i + 1 = pellP (n + 1) + pellP n := by
  induction n with
  | zero => decide
  | succ k ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, Nat.mul_add, Nat.add_right_comm, ih]
      have h1 : pellP (k + 1 + 1) = 2 * pellP (k + 1) + pellP k := pellP_add_two k
      omega

/-- Partial sums of squares of Pell numbers telescope into a product. -/
theorem pellP_sq_sum (n : ℕ) :
    2 * ∑ i ∈ range (n + 1), pellP i ^ 2 = pellP n * pellP (n + 1) := by
  induction n with
  | zero => decide
  | succ k ih =>
      rw [Finset.sum_range_succ, Nat.mul_add, ih]
      have h1 : pellP (k + 1 + 1) = 2 * pellP (k + 1) + pellP k := pellP_add_two k
      rw [h1]
      ring

/-- One Euclidean step: `gcd (P (m+n)) (P n) = gcd (P m) (P n)`.
The addition law turns `P (m+n)` into `P m * Q n + Q m * P n`; the second summand is
killed modulo `P n`, and `Q n` is coprime to `P n`. -/
theorem pellP_gcd_step (m n : ℕ) :
    Nat.gcd (pellP (m + n)) (pellP n) = Nat.gcd (pellP m) (pellP n) := by
  have hco : Nat.Coprime (pellQ n) (pellP n) :=
    Nat.Coprime.symm (pellP_coprime_pellQ n)
  calc Nat.gcd (pellP (m + n)) (pellP n)
      = Nat.gcd (pellP m * pellQ n + pellP n * pellQ m) (pellP n) := by
        rw [pellP_add]; ring_nf
    _ = Nat.gcd (pellP m * pellQ n) (pellP n) :=
        Nat.gcd_add_mul_left_left _ _ _
    _ = Nat.gcd (pellP m) (pellP n) := hco.gcd_mul_right_cancel _

/-- Iterated Euclidean step: multiples of the index may be discarded. -/
theorem pellP_gcd_mul_step (q m r : ℕ) :
    Nat.gcd (pellP (m * q + r)) (pellP m) = Nat.gcd (pellP r) (pellP m) := by
  induction q with
  | zero => simp
  | succ q ih =>
      have : m * (q + 1) + r = (m * q + r) + m := by ring
      rw [this, pellP_gcd_step, ih]

/-- **Strong divisibility of the Pell spine**: `gcd (P m) (P n) = P (gcd m n)`.

theorem pellP_gcd (m n : ℕ) : Nat.gcd (pellP m) (pellP n) = pellP (Nat.gcd m n) := by
  induction m using Nat.strong_induction_on generalizing n with
  | _ m ih =>
      rcases Nat.eq_zero_or_pos m with rfl | hm
      · simp
      · have hr : n % m < m := Nat.mod_lt _ hm
        have hsplit : m * (n / m) + n % m = n := by
          rw [Nat.mul_comm]; exact Nat.div_add_mod' n m
        calc Nat.gcd (pellP m) (pellP n)
            = Nat.gcd (pellP n) (pellP m) := Nat.gcd_comm _ _
          _ = Nat.gcd (pellP (m * (n / m) + n % m)) (pellP m) := by rw [hsplit]
          _ = Nat.gcd (pellP (n % m)) (pellP m) := pellP_gcd_mul_step _ _ _
          _ = pellP (Nat.gcd (n % m) m) := ih _ hr m
          _ = pellP (Nat.gcd m n) := by rw [← Nat.gcd_rec]

      rw [pellP_gcd, Nat.gcd_eq_left_iff_dvd.mpr h]
    exact Nat.gcd_eq_left_iff_dvd.mp this
  · intro h
    have h1 : Nat.gcd (pellP m) (pellP n) = pellP m := Nat.gcd_eq_left_iff_dvd.mpr h
    rw [pellP_gcd] at h1

    exact Nat.gcd_eq_left_iff_dvd.mp this

  rcases (Nat.Prime.eq_one_or_self_of_dvd h _ hdvd) with h1 | h1 <;> omega

        print(f"{p:>5} {p % 8:>8} {legendre_two(p):>6} {r:>8} {side:>12}"
              f"  {'confirmed' if euler_ok else 'FAILED':>26}")
    print()
    print("   The side is predicted by the Legendre symbol (2/p): rank divides p - (2/p).")
    print("   Naive guess 'rank(p) | p-1' dies at p = 3, where rank(3) = 4 and 4 does")
    print("   not divide 2 -- but 4 does divide p+1 = 4, exactly as the law demands.")
    print()


def show_wall_sun_sun(bound: int = 4000) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("6. PELL-WALL-SUN-SUN PRIMES:  p^2 | P(rank(p))")
    print("=" * 74)
    hits: List[int] = []
    for p in range(3, bound + 1):
        if not is_prime(p):
            continue
        r = pell_rank(p)
        if pell_P_mod(r, p * p) == 0:
            hits.append(p)
            print(f"   p = {p:>5}: rank(p) = rank(p^2) = {r},  P({r}) = {pell_P(r)}")
    print(f"   Pell-Wall-Sun-Sun primes below {bound}: {hits}")
    print("   Consequently the Wall-Sun-Sun growth law rank(p^2) = p * rank(p) is FALSE:")
    print(f"     rank(13)  = {pell_rank(13)},  rank(169) = {pell_rank(169)}"
          f"   (P(7) = {pell_P(7)} = 13^2)")
    print(f"     rank(31)  = {pell_rank(31)},  rank(961) = {pell_rank(961)}"
          f"   (31^2 | P(30) = {pell_P(30)})")
    print("   For Fibonacci numbers no analogous prime is known at all.")
    print()


def show_p7_singularity() -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("7. P(7) = 169: A SINGLE POINT OF FAILURE")
    print("=" * 74)
    p7 = pell_P(7)
    print(f"   P(7) = {p7} = 13^2, at the prime index 7.")
    print(f"     prime index => prime value?  {is_prime(p7)}  (refuted)")
    print(f"     Pell numbers squarefree?     {is_squarefree(p7)}  (refuted)")
    print(f"     no Pell number a square?     {not is_square(p7)}  (refuted)")
    print(f"     near-isosceles hypotenuse prime?  119^2 + 120^2 = {119**2 + 120**2}"
          f" = {p7}^1, and {p7} = 13^2  (refuted)")
    print(f"     13 a Pell-Wall-Sun-Sun prime?  {pell_rank(169) == pell_rank(13)}"
          f"  (yes -- same term)")
    print()


def show_near_isosceles(count: int = 7) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("8. NEAR-ISOSCELES PYTHAGOREAN TRIPLES  a^2 + (a+1)^2 = c^2")
    print("=" * 74)
    print(f"{'k':>3} {'a':>12} {'a+1':>12} {'c = P(2k+1)':>14} {'c mod 4':>8}")
    for k in range(count):
        idx = 2 * k + 1
        q, c = pell_pair(idx)
        a = (q - 1) // 2
        assert a * a + (a + 1) ** 2 == c * c
        print(f"{k:>3} {a:>12} {a+1:>12} {c:>14} {c % 4:>8}")
    print("   Every such triple arises this way, and every hypotenuse is 1 mod 4.")
    print("   The k = 3 row is (119, 120, 169) -- the hypotenuse 169 = 13^2 is composite.")
    print()


def show_unit_classification(bound: int = 200) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("9. CLASSIFICATION OF x^2 - 2y^2 = +-1")
    print("=" * 74)
    spine = {(pell_Q(n), pell_P(n)) for n in range(0, 12)}
    found: List[Tuple[int, int, int]] = []
    for x in range(0, bound + 1):
        for y in range(0, bound + 1):
            d = x * x - 2 * y * y
            if d in (1, -1):
                found.append((x, y, d))
    on_spine = all((x, y) in spine for x, y, _ in found)
    print(f"   brute-force solutions with 0 <= x,y <= {bound}: {[(x, y) for x, y, _ in found]}")
    print(f"   all lie on the spine: {on_spine}")
    print("   sign of the norm = parity of the index: +1 for even n, -1 for odd n.")
    print(f"   x^2 = 2y^2 + 3 has no solution at all (obstruction mod 8):"
          f" {not any((x*x - 2*y*y) == 3 for x in range(bound) for y in range(bound))}")
    print(f"   but x^2 - 2y^2 = 7 does have one: 3^2 - 2*1^2 = {3*3 - 2*1}")
    print()


def show_approximation(n: int = 14) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("10. APPROXIMATION OF sqrt2:  |Q(n) - P(n) sqrt2| = (sqrt2 - 1)^n")
    print("=" * 74)
    from decimal import Decimal, getcontext

    getcontext().prec = 50
    root2 = Decimal(2).sqrt()
    print(f"{'n':>3} {'|Q - P sqrt2|':>22} {'(sqrt2-1)^n':>22} {'|sqrt2 - Q/P| * P^2':>22}")
    for k in range(1, n + 1):
        q, p = pell_pair(k)
        err = abs(Decimal(q) - Decimal(p) * root2)
        geo = (root2 - 1) ** k
        scaled = abs(root2 - Decimal(q) / Decimal(p)) * Decimal(p) ** 2
        print(f"{k:>3} {str(err)[:22]:>22} {str(geo)[:22]:>22} {str(scaled)[:22]:>22}")
    print("   The last column is < 1 for every n >= 1 (Dirichlet quality),")
    print("   but at n = 1 it equals 0.414... > 1/3, so the constant 1 is not")
    print("   improvable to 1/3 on the whole spine.")
    print()


def show_identities(n: int = 15) -> None:
    print("=" * 74)
    print("11. IDENTITIES TYING THE TWO STRANDS TOGETHER")
    print("=" * 74)
    ok_sum_q = all(sum(pell_Q(i) for i in range(k + 1)) == pell_P(k + 1)
                   for k in range(n))
    ok_sum_p = all(2 * sum(pell_P(i) for i in range(k + 1)) + 1
                   == pell_P(k + 1) + pell_P(k) for k in range(n))
    ok_sum_sq = all(2 * sum(pell_P(i) ** 2 for i in range(k + 1))
                    == pell_P(k) * pell_P(k + 1) for k in range(n))
    ok_cassini = all(pell_P(k + 2) * pell_P(k) - pell_P(k + 1) ** 2 == (-1) ** (k + 1)
                     for k in range(n))
    print(f"   sum_{{i<=n}} Q(i) = P(n+1)                        : {ok_sum_q}")
    print(f"   2 sum_{{i<=n}} P(i) + 1 = P(n+1) + P(n)           : {ok_sum_p}")
    print(f"   2 sum_{{i<=n}} P(i)^2 = P(n) P(n+1)               : {ok_sum_sq}")
    print(f"   Cassini: P(n+2)P(n) - P(n+1)^2 = (-1)^(n+1)     : {ok_cassini}")
    print()


def rank_table(bound: int = 40) -> Dict[int, int]:
    return {m: pell_rank(m) for m in range(1, bound + 1)}


def main() -> None:
    show_spine()
    show_strong_divisibility()
    show_companion_law()
    show_apparition()
    show_fermat_law()
    show_wall_sun_sun()
    show_p7_singularity()
    show_near_isosceles()
    show_unit_classification()
    show_approximation()
    show_identities()
    print("=" * 74)
    print("All demonstrations completed.")
    print("=" * 74)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

# Phase A Research Mission v19c: The dichotomy, the local homeomorphism property and the semicontinuity

            **Domain**: Tropical | **Mode**: team
            **Description**: The dichotomy, the local homeomorphism property and the semicontinuity
of `sheetNumber` are all proved; the remaining step is to run the same
trivialisation argument relative to an open subset of the base.
            **Mathematical Framing**: The dichotomy, the local homeomorphism property and the semicontinuity
of `sheetNumber` are all proved; the remaining step is to run the same
trivialisation argument relative to an open subset of the base.



            ## v19 Research Core Methodology — Speculative Scientific-Method Loop

You are the Principal Investigator leading a speculative research team with four
roles: **Hypothesizer**, **Experimenter**, **Analyst**, and **Critic**. This engine
is configured for **Speculative Specifying (Bold Conjectures)**: target high-risk,
high-reward, grand-challenge level research while maintaining adversarial rigor.

### Stage 1 — Hypothesize (team: Hypothesizer)
Brainstorm 5–7 falsifiable conjectures about the topic. At least three must be
bold, surprising, or grand-challenge level. Rank them by expected scientific
impact, not by ease of proof.
**CRITICAL SCORING REQUIREMENT**: To maximize your Phase A quality score, your
conjectures MUST aim for extreme `proof_depth` (deep structural hierarchies rather
than shallow one-liners) and `cross_domain` bridging (combining distinct areas of
math, e.g., algebra with topology, or geometry with combinatorics).

### Stage 2 — Experiment (team: Experimenter)
For each conjecture, attempt to prove it in Lean 4 or disprove it with a concrete
counterexample. Prioritize the boldest conjectures first. If a proof is beyond
reach, prove the strongest lemma you can and mark the remaining step with exactly
one `sorry` that is clearly documented.

### Stage 3 — Analyze (team: Analyst)
Summarize what survived, what failed, and **why** failures failed. Distinguish
"true but hard", "false", and "needs a different definition". Extract structural
patterns that could unify several observations.

### Stage 4 — Critique / Adversarial Review (team: Critic)
Before finalizing, challenge every theorem:
- Is any theorem trivial (True, definitional equality, `native_decide`)?
- Does every main theorem have 0 sorries?
- Do the results genuinely extend the attached catalog files?
- Are there hidden assumptions or corner cases that break the claim?
If you find a weakness, fix it or replace the theorem with a guarded version and
explain the boundary.

### Stage 5 — Synthesize (team: Principal Investigator)
Combine the verified results into clean, compiling Lean 4 files.
Write a `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md` that lists 3–5 **bold, testable** conjectures
derived from Stage 3 and Stage 4. Each conjecture must include a
"The key insight is..." sentence and a "Why now?" justification.

ADDITIONALLY — machine-readable directions block (REQUIRED). In
FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md, after the prose sections, emit a fenced JSON
array named future_directions.json with one object per direction
(3–6 entries), each with exactly these keys:
```json
[{"title": "<short noun-phrase name, NOT a sentence>",
  "domain": "<one of: NumberTheory, Algebra, Geometry, Combinatorics, Computation, Physics, Probability, Cryptography, Logic, MachineLearning, Tropical, Bridges>",
  "description": "<2-4 sentences: the conjecture, the approach, why it matters>",
  "conjecture": "<the precise mathematical claim>",
  "test": "<how to test or formalize it>",
  "if_true": "<consequence if true>",
  "if_false": "<consequence if false>",
  "proof_strategy": "<sketch of the proof route>",
  "catalog_references": ["<Catalog.lean.module>"]}]

Titles must be noun phrases ("Silver-Ratio Spectral Gap for Pell Spines"),
never sentences or recaps ("This cycle proved..." is forbidden).

### Perpetual Scientific Iteration (do not stop at first synthesis)
When the research team comes together with results, do not stop. Treat the
synthesized findings as the next problem statement and immediately run the full
scientific-method loop again: hypothesize, experiment, review, synthesize,
critique. Repeat this cycle continuously within the available context window,
refining, deepening, and cross-checking until forced to emit output. Use
Aristotle to its fullest.

### Anti-Trivial Guardrails
- Do not produce trivial proofs (`True := by trivial`, `rfl`-only, `Inhabited X`-only, `native_decide`-only).
- Use an insight-bearing tactic (e.g. `induction`, `nlinarith`, `omega`, `field_simp`).

### Self-Critique Checklist
- No theorem is trivial.
- Every main theorem has 0 sorries.
- Lab Notes blocks contain real experimental data.

### Strictly Forbidden in Phase A
Do NOT create packaging deliverables in Phase A: `ARTICLE.md`, `RESEARCH_PAPER.md`, `demo.py`, `PACKAGE.json`.

### Recursive Abduction / Thread Continuation (v19c)
If prior-cycle context is provided, treat it as a live research thread: refine
the hypotheses from the previous cycle, attempt to close open conjectures, and
produce three concrete next-cycle sub-conjectures. If no prior context is
provided, still run a self-contained abductive loop: generate conjectures, test
them, and immediately spin off the most promising follow-up conjectures as
future directions.


            ## Hard Constraints

Extended grid on French prose (corpus-B; gate exact):

| k | 36 | 40 | 48 | 56 | 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| retained | 0.9795 ✗ | **0.9830 ✓** | 0.9855 ✓ | 0.9896 ✓ | 0.9916 ✓ |

**k\*(fr@1024) = 40 — exactly DOUBLE English prose's 20 at the same context.**

code=12, EN-prose=20, math=20, DE-prose=24, FR-prose=40. The tokenizer-tax is a domain-dependent MULTIPLIER (German +4, French ×2), not a fixed +4 step. concept.title: Margin Scarcity as the Portability Predictor
concept.concept_description:
Two candidate predictors of transplant damage exist in the catalog: a norm-based upper bound and a margin-based certificate. Conjecture: the margin-uncertified fraction predicts damage, and Lipschitz/norm distance between the two copies of a block does not.

Across layer blocks, the measured post-transplant disagreement correlates with the margin-uncertified fraction and is not monotone in the block's weight-space distance.

Compute both predictors per block and compare against measured disagreement, using net54_margin_failure_fraction as the certified lower bound.

Portability becomes predictable from a cheap forward-pass statistic, with no transplant needed.

Norm-based bounds remain the operative predictor and the margin route is only a sufficient condition.
